summary: Specifies how PPP is used over SONET and SDH optical circuits. It replaced RFC 1619.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP carries network packets between two endpoints over a direct link. This document describes how to run it over the fibre-optic circuits called SONET or SDH, and adds a scrambler that stops anyone on the line forging a pattern that confuses the equipment.

questions: how does ppp work over sonet
what is the path signal label for ppp
subtitle: How PPP frames ride inside SONET/SDH optical circuits, with a self-synchronous scrambler to keep the line safe.

tldr.problem: PPP needs a well-defined way to enter and leave an optical circuit, and the earlier definition of that let an attacker inject bits that could break the line equipment.
tldr.mechanism: The document maps the PPP octet stream into the SONET or SDH container, scrambles the payload with a self-synchronous X^43 + 1 scrambler, and names the choice in the container's Path Signal Label.
tldr.outcome: The optical layer can no longer be confused by crafted bit patterns, and the payload is scrambled end to end across the container. The document replaced RFC 1619 in 1999.

facts.value: 32 bits, except that 16 bits may be used on STS-3c-SPE/VC-4

today: RFC 2615 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 1619 in 1999 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The PPP and PPP framing it relies on are defined in RFC 1661 and RFC 1662.

sections.title: Why PPP over SONET/SDH
sections.content:
PPP is a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over a point-to-point link. It was designed for short local lines, leased lines and plain telephone service with modems, and it is easily deployed as faster packet services and higher-speed lines appear.

This document is concerned with the use of the PPP encapsulation over SONET/SDH links. SONET and SDH are two names for what are essentially the same optical transmission standards, and the real differences between them, other than terminology, are minor; for the purposes of encapsulating PPP over them they are inconsequential. The document lists the equivalent terms side by side, and notes that only four container sizes are supported: STS-3c-SPE with VC-4, STS-12c-SPE with VC-4-4c, STS-48c-SPE with VC-4-16c, and STS-192c-SPE with VC-4-64c.

SONET/SDH is by definition a point-to-point circuit, which makes it well suited to PPP. The document replaces and obsoletes RFC 1619.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP carries network packets between two endpoints over a direct link. This document works out how to place those packets inside the fibre-optic containers called SONET or SDH.

sections.title: Mapping PPP onto the Optical Circuit
sections.content:
PPP treats SONET/SDH transport as an octet-oriented synchronous link, and SONET/SDH links are full duplex by definition. PPP in HDLC-like framing presents an octet interface to the physical layer; there is no provision for sub-octets to be supplied or accepted. The octet stream is mapped into the SONET STS-SPE or SDH Higher Order VC with the octet boundaries aligned with that container's octet boundaries.

The order of operation is fixed. When transmitting: IP, then PPP, then FCS generation, then byte stuffing, then scrambling, then SONET/SDH framing. When receiving: SONET/SDH framing, then descrambling, then byte destuffing, then FCS detection, then PPP, then IP.

The Path Signal Label (C2) indicates the contents of the container. The value 22 (16 hex) is used to indicate PPP with X^43 + 1 scrambling. For compatibility with RFC 1619, which covered only STS-3c-SPE/VC-4, the scrambler may have an on/off capability, in which case the default must be scrambling enabled and the value 207 (CF hex) indicates PPP without scrambling. The Multiframe Indicator (H4) is unused and must be zero.

The PPP frames are located by row within the container payload. Because frames are variable in length, they are allowed to cross container boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: On the way out, the packet is framed, checked, escaped and then scrambled before it goes into the optical container. On the way in, those steps run in reverse. One label byte in the container says which of these is being done.

sections.title: The X^43 + 1 Scrambler
sections.content:
The scrambler is a self-synchronous device built around a 43-bit shift register. On transmit, the data is exclusive-ORed with the output of the register and fed back into it. On receive, the scrambled data is exclusive-ORed with the register output to recover the original. The scrambler operates continuously through the bytes of the container, bypassing the SONET path overhead and any fixed stuff.

The bit order is worth noting. The HDLC frame check sequence is calculated least significant bit first, so the calculator is fed A[0], A[1] and so on, and A[7], A[6] and so on for the next byte. Scrambling is done the opposite way, most significant bit first, so the scrambler is fed A[7], A[6], A[5] and so on.

The scrambler runs continuously and is not reset per frame. The state at the beginning of a container is the state at the end of the previous one, and the initial seed is chosen at random by the transmitter. One consequence is that the first 43 transmitted bits following startup or a reframe operation will not be descrambled correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: The scrambler shifts the data through a 43-bit register and mixes in the bits it remembers, so the output looks nothing like the input. Both ends run the same device in reverse to get the data back.

sections.title: Configuration Details
sections.content:
Other than the frame check sequence length, the standard LCP synchronisation configuration defaults apply to SONET/SDH links.

For STS-3c-SPE/VC-4 the recommended configuration options are the Magic Number, no Address and Control Field Compression, and no Protocol Field Compression. For operation at STS-12c-SPE/VC-4-4c and above, Address and Control Field Compression and Protocol Field Compression are not recommended, and the Magic Number option remains recommended.

Regarding the FCS length, with one exception the 32-bit FCS must be used for all SONET/SDH rates. For STS-3c-SPE/VC-4 only, the 16-bit FCS may be used, although the 32-bit FCS is recommended. The FCS length is set by provisioning and is not negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: Most PPP link settings work unchanged. The two that matter here are how long the error check is and whether the header fields are compressed, and the recommendation is the longer check and uncompressed headers at higher rates.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The major change from RFC 1619 is the addition of payload scrambling when the framed PPP packets are inserted into the container. RFC 1619 was found in operation to permit malicious users to generate packets with bit patterns that could create SONET/SDH-layer low-transition-density synchronisation problems, emulation of the SDH set-reset scrambler pattern, and replication of the STM-N frame alignment word.

The X^43 + 1 self-synchronous scrambler was introduced to reduce these problems. Predicting its output requires knowledge of the 43-bit state of the transmitter when the scrambling of a known input began, and of every byte of data scrambled since. The odds of guessing correctly are 1 in 2^43, with an additional probability of 1 in 127 that a correct guess leaves the frame properly aligned in the payload, which gives a probability of 9e-16 of deliberately causing layer problems. The document judges this reasonably secure for this application, and notes that the same scrambler is used when transmitting ATM over SONET/SDH and that public network carriers have considerable experience with it.

A known security issue remains: a user can cause up to a 100% increase in the bandwidth required for their packets by filling the packet with flag and escape characters, which need transparency processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Without scrambling, someone on the line could craft bits that break the optical equipment's synchronisation. The scrambler turns that into guesswork: the odds of getting it right are about one in 10 to the 15. A user can still waste bandwidth on purpose by sending characters that need escaping.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 1619
sections.content:
The document lists the changes from RFC 1619. Beyond the addition of payload scrambling, the terminology was updated to match that used by ANSI and ITU-T. The specification's applicability is now restricted to four pairs: STS-3c-SPE with VC-4, STS-12c-SPE with VC-4-4c, STS-48c-SPE with VC-4-16c, and STS-192c-SPE with VC-4-64c.

The Path Signal Label (C2) is set to 22 (16 hex) when X^43 + 1 scrambling is used. The 32-bit FCS is required except for operation with STS-3c-SPE/VC-4, in which case the 16-bit FCS is allowed, though the 32-bit FCS is still recommended. A Security Considerations section was added.
sections.plainLanguage: The 1999 version of this document adds the scrambler, tightens the list of supported circuit sizes, requires the longer error check almost everywhere, and explains the security reasoning for the first time.
